Rafique-ul-Huq with Shafiq Ahmed, Tawfique Nawaz, Ahsanul Karim, Faheemul Huq, Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh, Md Mehedi Hasan Chowdhury Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
M Salahuddin Ahmed and Mansur Habib, Additional Attorneys-General Syeda Afsar Jahan, Deputy Attorneys-General—For the Respondents. 
TH Khan, Abdur Rab Chaudhury, Mahbubur Rahman, Md Rafiqul Islam Miah, Mahbubey Alam, Md Munsurul Hoque Chowdhury, Advocates—Amici.
parties:
Sheikh Hasina alias Sheikh Hasina Wazed ------ Petitioner
vs
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary Ministry of Home Affairs and others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
SAN Mominur Rahman J: The Rule was issued upon the respondents to show cause as to why the sanction given by the respondent No. 2, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh, vide Memo No. স্বঃমঃ(আইন-১)/জক্ষবি-১/০৭(অংশ-৫)/৭১২ dated 16-7-2007 purportedly under Rule-19ঞ(২) of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, for proceeding with Gulshan Police Station Case No. 34 dated 13-6-2007 filed under sections 385/109 of the Penal Code, 1860, under the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, treating the offence alleged to be of public importance, evidenced by the Annexure-C to the Writ Petition, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 (c) in the year 2000 AD the company of the informant, acting on behalf of Messrs Techno prom Export, a Russian firm, (hereinafter referred to as "TPE"), participated in a tender and obtained the work order for "First Phase of the Erection and Commissioning of a Power Plant" at Siddhirganj Power Station, Narayanganj, and that while the project work was progressing, Sheikh Fazlul Karim Selim started pressurizing the informant for illegal payment of money and in the month of July 2000, the informant agreed to pay and that the alleged payment was made in between the period October, 2000 and March, 2001 AD, through cheques, by the informant personally and that section 385 of the Penal Code, 1860 is not attracted in the face of the allegations as made in the written ejahar, since there is no ingredient of extortion, defined in section 383 of the Penal Code, 1860, that the police after investigation submitted its report (charge sheet) bearing No. 27 dated 23-7-2007 under sections 385/109/34 of the Penal Code, 1860, and that impugned sanction under Rule 190 of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 (hereinafter referred to as EPR) was given by the respondent No. 2, for proceeding with the case under the EPR, without fulfilling the condition-precedent, set down by Rule 19ঞ(4) of the EPR, that is, the sanctioning authority must be "satisfied that the offence alleged is of public importance", and that the impugned sanction as given is arbitrary, malafide and has been given without considering the gravity of the "offence alleged" but considering the status of the accused and that the Rule-19ঞ of the EPR is bad, inasmuch as the sanctioning authority has been given arbitrary and unfettered discretion to "pick and choose" and there is no guideline for determining which offence can be treated as "offence of public importance" and that the impugned sanction as given is a malafide and colorable exercise of power to harass and cause loss to the accused and that the case has been approved for proceeding under the EPR, with the ulterior motive to treat the accused harshly, and to deprive her from getting fair justice and bail, which is available under the normal law, and that the Court has the authority to test the validity of Rule 19ঞ and other provisions in the EPR debarring the grant of bail to an accused, since those are inconsistent with the Articles guaranteeing the fundamental rights detailed in Part III of the Constitution and void in view of Article 26(2) thereof; and 

 (d) Sheikh Fazlul Karim Selim, cousin of the accused petitioner, has been made accused No. 1 in the case and a forceful confessional statement was extracted from said Sheikh Fazlul Karim Selim under torture, threat, coercion, duress and intimidation, by members of the Joint Forces, while he was under custody, on remand, and that other charge sheet bearing No. 501 dated 30-11-2007 has been submitted adding the offence under section 384 of the Penal Code, 1860, and that said Sheikh Fazlul Karim Selim, on getting first opportunity, retracted the said confessional statement, both orally and in writing, when produced in the Court, and that the accused petitioner by filing an application under section 265C of the Code of Criminal Procedure prayed for her discharge from the case but the prayer was rejected without considering the provisions of section 3(৩ক) of the Emergency Power Ordinance; 2007 (hereinafter referred to as EPO) and Article 93 of the Constitution, and that the case is being proceeded with illegally, since the alleged offence was said to have been committed prior to the promulgation of the Emergency and thus hits section 3(৩ক) of the EPO and Article 93 of the Constitution, and that the provisions of Rule 1917 and 19G of the EPR, so far infringes the right of the accused petitioner to pray for bail, are void being inconsistent with the provisions of the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, which are not suspended or affected by Article 141B of the Constitution and thus, the proceeding of the case under the EPR, pursuant to the impugned sanction, is bad in the eye of law. Certified copy of (1) the application filed under section 265C of the CrPC, (2) the application retracting the confessional statement of Sheikh Fazlul Karim Selim, (3) the statements recorded under section 161 of the CrPC, (4) FIR, (5) Charge Sheet No. 271 dated 23-7-2007, (6) Supplementary Charge Sheet No. 312 dated 18-8-2007, and (7) Supplementary Sheet No. 501 dated 30-11-2007 have been annexed to the Writ Petition and the Supplementary Affidavit of the petitioner. 

 10. The learned Advocate, in support of his contention that the Rule 19ঞ of the Rules, 2007, relating to the authority to give sanction for proceeding with a case under the EPR is bad, since there is scope for discriminatory use, as no guideline is given and the authority has been given unfettered and unguided power, referred to the decisions in the cases of (i) Waris Mea vs State, reported in 9 DLR (SC) 117; (ii) Mustafa Kamal vs Commissioner of Customs and others, reported in 2000 BLD (AD) 1 = 52 DLR (AD) 1; (iii) Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh, reported in 33 DLR (AD) 201; and (iv) Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin Ahmed and others, reported in 50 DLR (AD)27. 

 38. Apart from this, our Courts also decided several cases on the question of retrospective effect and in particular, as has been referred to before us, in the case of (i) Registrar, University of Dhaka vs Dr Syed Sajjad Hussain and others, reported in 34 DLR (AD) 1, wherein their Lordships in deciding a case under President's Order No. 67 of 1972 referring to the words used in President's Order No. 8 of 1972, arrived at a decision that the alleged acts of the petitioner cannot be considered under President's Order No. 67 of 1972, which law is prospective, and has the protection of Article 35 of the Constitution and that "it is well settled that if the enactment is expressed in language which is fairly capable of either interpretation, it ought to be construed as prospective only, specially when a penal statute is required to be construed." In the case of Arjan Singh and another vs State of Punjab and others, reported in AIR 1970 (SC) 703, cited by Mr Md Munsurul Hoque Chowdhury, the learned Advocate, wherein their Lordships observed that "it is a well-settled rule of construction that no provision in a statute should be given retrospective effect unless the legislature by express terms or by necessary implication has made it retrospective and that where a provision is made retrospective, care should be taken not to extend its retrospective effect beyond what was intended." 

 39. On the point of interpreting "provisions of the Constitution or any Statute" the learned Advocate Mr Tawfique Nawaz placed before us a list of cases, decisions of which have been reported in Dhaka Law Reports (DLR) and Bangladesh Legal Decisions (BLD), during the period 1957 to 2002, of which we only relied on the following cases namely, (1) in the matter of Reference by the President of Pakistan under Article 162 of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, reported in 9 DLR (SC) 178, (2) Abdul Kader vs Secretary Election Commission and others, reported in 58 DLR (AD) 71, (3) Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission vs Ekushey Television Ltd., reported in 58 DLR (AD) 82; (4) National Board of Revenue vs Nasrin Banu, reported in 48 DLR (AD) 176, (5) Bangladesh vs Dhaka Steel Works Ltd., reported in 45 DLR (AD) 79, (5) Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh, reported in 33 DLR (AD) 253, (6) Ahmed Hossain vs Bashrat Ali, reported in 32 DLR (AD) 57, (7) Commissioner of Income Tax vs M/s Gulistan Cinema Co reported in 28 DLR (AD) 18, (8) Md Ismail vs State, reported in 21 DLR (SC) 164, (9) Khizir Hayat Khan Eusuf Zai vs Major (Rtd) Md Muqtadir Ali, reported in 2000 BLD (AD) 46 = 4 BLC (AD) 100, (10) Mohammad Ali Akhand vs Bahatan Nessa Bewa and others, reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 50 = 3 BLC (AD) 177, (11) Md Mujibur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 1992 BLD (AD) 97 = 44 DLR (AD) 111, (12) and in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Mozibur Rahman and others, reported in 1992 BLD (AD) 284 = 44 DLR (AD) 90, (13) Abdul Hai Khan vs State, reported in 1988 BLD (AD) 195 = 40 DLR (AD) 226 and (14) Bangladesh vs Haji Abdul Gani Biswas, reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 8 = 32 DLR (AD) 233, to substantiate the principle that plain meaning should be given in interpreting any Statute, when the language is clear and unambiguous. The learned Advocate also cited the case of Solicitor vs Syed Sanwar Ali, reported in 27 DLR (AD) 21 (page 16 in reprinted copy), to substantiate the contention that where the words used in a law are "clear and unambiguous", Courts are to apply the same law as is understood, even if such application causes hardship and injustice. Further, in the case of Ismail, reported in 21 DLR (SC) 161 their Lordships held that Courts are not concerned with the consequences of the interpretation, however drastic or inconvenient the function of the Court is interpretation and not legislation. We are in respectful agreement with the aforesaid decisions and accordingly, we have also interpreted the provisions of the Constitution, the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Emergency Power Ordinance, 2007, Emergency Power Rules, 2007 and the Proclamation of Emergency, Order Nos. 1 and 2 of 2007 in reference in arriving at our decision. 

 40. The provisions of EPO are clear and unambiguous. It has given the authority to the Government to frame rules for the purpose of implementation and execution of the provisions set down in section 3(1) of EPO. The Rule making authority has not been given the authority to frame any rule beyond the scope of the Ordinance itself. Thus having regard to the reasoning’s given in support of the opinions of the learned Amici Curiae, and the submissions of the learned Advocates of the contesting parties and on analyzing the provisions of the EPO, the EPR and the relevant provisions of the Constitution, referred to above, we are of the view that neither the Constitution nor the EPO has provided any authority to the government to frame Rules or any part thereof giving retrospective effect thereon and therefore, by the EPR, framed under the authority of the EPO, the offences committed prior to the 11th January 2007 cannot be proceeded with or tried under the provisions of Emergency Power Rules, 2007 and for that matter no sanction can be given for the purpose of investigation, trial, etc. of the cases arising out of the offences committed prior to the Emergency. It is also a settled law that when there is a conflict between the law and rule framed under such law, the provisions of law will prevail, and this view gets support from the decision in the case of Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin Ahmed and others, reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27. Hence the provisions of EPR cannot override the provisions of EPO. 

 43. Though Mr Mahmudul Islam expressed his inability to assist the Court because of his personal difficulty, we may profitably refer to his submissions made in the case of lqbal Hasan Mahmood alias lqbal Hasan Mahmood Tuku vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 60 DLR 88, appearing as Amicus Curiae, which has been recorded in the said judgment, delivered on 5-12-2007, and the relevant portion is quoted below: 

 53. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned sanction given by the respondent No. 2 under Rule 19ঞ (2) of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, vide Memo No. স্বঃমঃ(আইন-১)/জক্ষবি-১/০৭/(অংশ-৫)/৭১২ dated 16-7-2007, for proceeding with the Gulshan Police Station Case No. 34 dated 13-6-2007 filed under sections 385/109 of the Penal Code, 1860, under the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 treating the offence to be of public importance, evidenced by the Annexure-C to the Writ petition, is declared to be without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and consequently, any action taken and or initiation and continuation of any proceeding and or trial of any case, arising out of said Gulshan Police Station Case No. 34 dated 13-6-2007, under the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, in any Court of law or authority, is declared to be without lawful authority, and stands quashed.
